title: Financing of Working Capital
outcomes: Identify spontaneous, short-term and long-term sources of working capital.
Evaluate commercial paper, bill discounting and ICDs.
Explain forms and assessment of bank working capital finance.

meta.exam_tip: Annualise every short-term cost before comparing sources.

concepts.title: Sources of working capital finance
body: Spontaneous sources: trade credit and accrued expenses (wages, taxes) that rise with activity.

Short-term sources: bank cash credit and overdraft, working capital demand loans, bill discounting, commercial paper, inter-corporate deposits, factoring, advances from customers, and public deposits (subject to law).
Long-term sources (for permanent working capital): equity, retained earnings, long-term loans and debentures. The mix follows the firm's financing approach (matching, conservative or aggressive).
concepts.analogy: Use spontaneous credit first, short-term finance for swings and long-term funds for the base.
concepts.work: Advance payments from customers fund a builder's construction working capital.

concepts.title: Money market instruments: commercial paper, bills, ICDs
body: Commercial paper: an unsecured promissory note issued at a discount by highly rated companies; maturity from 7 days to less than one year; issued in denominations of ₹5 lakh or multiples; cheaper than bank credit for strong borrowers and repayable by rolling over.

Bill discounting: a bank pays the drawer the present value of a trade bill before maturity; cost is the discount charged. Inter-corporate deposits: short-term loans between companies, quick but costlier and riskier.
Certificates of deposit are issued by banks; treasury bills by the Government — these are investment rather than borrowing options for companies.
concepts.analogy: The money market lets strong companies borrow directly from investors for short periods.
concepts.work: A company with a top short-term rating raises ₹50 crore through 90-day CP below its bank rate.

concepts.title: Bank finance for working capital
body: Forms of bank finance: cash credit (borrow up to a limit against hypothecated stock and debtors, interest on amount used); overdraft; working capital demand loan; bills purchased or discounted; letters of credit and bank guarantees (non-fund-based).

Assessment: the Tandon Committee introduced maximum permissible bank finance (MPBF) with three methods, and the Chore Committee suggested separating limits into loan and cash credit components. RBI withdrew MPBF in 1997; banks now use Board-approved methods such as the projected balance sheet method, turnover method (for smaller borrowers) and cash budget method.
Banks require a margin (borrower's contribution), security, periodic stock statements and drawing power checks.
concepts.analogy: Banks fund the gap between current assets and spontaneous credit, after the borrower puts in a margin.
concepts.work: A cash credit limit of ₹5 crore with drawing power of ₹4 crore lets the borrower draw only ₹4 crore.

illustrations.title: Cost of commercial paper
illustrations.q: A highly rated company issues 90-day commercial paper of face value ₹100 at ₹97.50. Issue and rating costs add about 0.5% a year. Compute the effective annual cost and compare with a 12% cash credit.

solution.text: At about 10.9%, CP is cheaper than the 12% cash credit, so the company should use CP for part of its seasonal needs, keeping bank lines as back-up.

illustrations.title: How much will the bank lend?
illustrations.q: A borrower's projected current assets are ₹400 lakh and current liabilities other than bank borrowings ₹120 lakh. Using the Tandon Committee methods (now historical, as RBI lets banks set their own methods), compute maximum permissible bank finance under Method I and Method II.

head: Method
Working
₹ lakh
rows: 75% of current assets − other current liabilities
solution.title: MPBF (Tandon)

solution.text: Method II requires the borrower to fund 25% of total current assets from long-term sources, giving a lower bank limit.

checks.label: Method II: 75% of current assets − current liabilities (other than bank)
Method I: 75% of (current assets − current liabilities)

jobs.title: Funding plan for peak season
jobs.situation: A company needs ₹20 crore extra for three months each year.
steps: Estimate the size and timing of the peak need.
Compare cost of CP, cash credit and bill discounting.
Check credit rating and bank limits.
Recommend a mix with back-up lines.
jobs.takeaway: Cheapest is not enough — keep a reliable back-up for rollover risk.

mcqs.explain: Trade credit grows naturally with purchases. In practice: accrued wages are another example.

viva.model: An unsecured short-term promissory note issued at a discount by highly rated companies to raise funds from investors.
Trade credit from suppliers and accrued expenses such as outstanding wages and taxes.
A bank facility allowing borrowing up to a limit against hypothecation of stock and receivables, with interest only on the amount used.

viva.q: What did the Tandon Committee recommend?
viva.model: Norms for inventory and receivables and the concept of maximum permissible bank finance with three methods requiring rising borrower contribution.

viva.q: How do banks assess working capital today?
viva.model: Using Board-approved methods such as the projected balance sheet, turnover or cash budget method, within RBI prudential norms.

cases.title: Vertex Chemicals
cases.case: Vertex Chemicals (top short-term rating) has projected current assets of ₹300 crore and other current liabilities of ₹90 crore. Its bank charges 11.5% on cash credit. It can issue 180-day CP at ₹95 per ₹100 face value.

mcqs.explain: Current assets 300 − other current liabilities 90 = 210. In practice: bank and own funds fill this gap.

mcqs.q: MPBF under Tandon Method II (₹ crore):
mcqs.explain: 75% × 300 − 90 = 135. In practice: Method I would give 157.5.
5 ÷ 95 × 365 ÷ 180 = 10.67%. In practice: add issue costs before comparing.
